title: Jupiter's Great Red Spot | A Calm Journey Through Giant Storms to Sleep To
description:
Jupiter's Great Red Spot is the largest known storm in the solar system, a vast whirl of wind that has turned in the clouds of Jupiter for at least a century and a half, and probably far longer. In this calm, slow documentary we drift down through its clouds, follow the story of how it was discovered and measured, and then travel on to the storms of Saturn, Uranus and Neptune to see what weather looks like on worlds without a surface.

Take your time and let the narration carry you. We stay with what the Hubble Space Telescope, Voyager, Galileo, Cassini, Juno and the James Webb Space Telescope have really measured, and we say plainly where the questions are still open. It is a gentle episode for relaxing, learning something real, and falling asleep to.
tags: calm space video to fall asleep
hook_promise: A single storm wider than Earth has been turning in Jupiter's clouds for at least 150 years, and the newest measurements show it is shrinking and reaching far deeper than anyone expected.

chapters.title: The Eye of Jupiter
chapters.question: What is that red oval staring back from the largest planet?
chapters.reveal: The Great Red Spot is a storm wide enough to swallow Earth, spinning in a counter-clockwise turn once every several Earth days.

Scale of the planet: more than eleven Earth diameters across
The Great Red Spot appears on the southern edge of a band
Its size today compared with Earth
Winds circle it counter-clockwise, which marks it as a high-pressure system
Plant the curiosity: how long has it been there, and why does it not die?
image_queries: Jupiter Great Red Spot close up
chapters.text:
Jupiter does not look like a planet at first. From far away, it looks like a small, striped marble, held very still against the dark.

As the distance closes, the stripes widen into bands. Cream and rust, pale brown and white, each one a river of cloud running east or west around the whole globe. The edges between them are not clean. They curl and fold into slow, feathered eddies, like cream stirred gently into tea.

Then the size begins to register. Jupiter is more than eleven Earth diameters across. If you lined up Earths along its middle, like beads on a string, it would take more than eleven of them to span it. A jet airliner crossing that distance would be flying for about seven days.

Look now toward the southern half of the planet, along the edge of one broad band. Something is there that does not belong to the pattern. A single oval, the color of old brick, sits among the pale clouds. It is not a shadow, and it is not a moon passing in front. It is part of the planet itself.

What is that red oval, staring back from the largest world in the solar system?

The answer comes slowly, as the camera moves closer. The oval is wider than anything we are used to calling a storm. Today it measures a little over one Earth across. That is roughly thirteen thousand kilometers, about the distance from London to Sydney by air. It is still getting smaller, and in the past it was larger. Even now, our whole planet could be set down inside it, with room to spare around the edges.

Above that oval, the clouds are not still. They are turning. Watch the edges of the red, and you can see the paler clouds sliding around it. The motion runs counter-clockwise. That direction is a clue, and it matters.

On Earth, a hurricane in the northern hemisphere turns counter-clockwise. But a hurricane is a low-pressure system, where air rushes in toward the center and rises. In the southern hemisphere, the same kind of storm turns clockwise. Here, in Jupiter's south, the spin runs counter-clockwise. So this storm cannot be a low.

It must be the opposite. A high-pressure system, an anticyclone, with air pressed down and spiraling outward at its center. On Earth, such systems bring calm, clear skies. On Jupiter, the same kind of turning has grown to a size we have no word for.

The winds along its rim are fast. They blow at hundreds of kilometers an hour, as fast as the most extreme storms on Earth. Yet the storm moves around in a slow, patient circle. One full turn takes about six Earth days.

So here is what we are looking at.

The Great Red Spot is a storm wide enough to swallow Earth, turning counter-clockwise once every six days or so.

It is a strange thing to hold in the mind. Our whole world, with its oceans and mountains and cities, would sit inside it like a stone in a bowl. And the storm would simply keep turning, with no sense that anything had changed.

That might be the end of the surprise. But a storm of that size raises a quieter question. On Earth, a hurricane lives for a week or two. It meets land, or cooler water, and it falls apart. This one has been turning for far longer than anyone has been counting.

How long has it been there? And why does it not die?

To begin to answer that, we have to look back, past the spacecraft and the cameras, to the first people who pointed a small glass at Jupiter and noticed that something was there.

chapters.title: Who Saw It First
chapters.question: Who first noticed this spot, and is it the same storm we see today?
chapters.reveal: Observers have recorded a spot on Jupiter since the seventeenth century, but the storm of today may not be the same one, and its continuous history reaches back at least to the eighteen-thirties.

Gaps in the historical record and the debate over a 'Permanent Spot'
Nineteenth-century drawings and the growing certainty it was a lasting feature
How the spot was much longer and larger in the past
Modern historians comparing old sketches with measurements
Open question: whether the earliest spot and today's storm are one and the same
image_queries: Jupiter Great Red Spot New Horizons
chapters.text:
In sixteen sixty-five, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini looked through a long, thin telescope at Jupiter and saw a dark spot on its face. He watched it for days, and he saw it drift slowly across the disk as the planet turned.

A spot on Jupiter. It sounds simple enough. But which spot was it, and is it the one we know?

The telescopes of that age were crude. Their lenses blurred color into fringes, and the views shook with every breath of wind. An observer might stand outside on a cold night for an hour, and come away with a single pencil sketch.

Cassini and others kept looking, and for a few years they kept noting a spot. Then the records thin out. For long stretches there is almost nothing, as if the planet had simply been forgotten.

That silence made some astronomers doubt. Perhaps these were not the same marking at all. Perhaps a spot had appeared, faded, and later another had formed in its place.

Some argued the opposite. They called it the Permanent Spot, a single feature that had stayed hidden in the gaps of the record. Neither side could prove it, because the sketches were too few and too rough.

Then, in the eighteen-thirties, the drawings grow more careful. An amateur observer in Germany, Samuel Heinrich Schwabe, sketched a clear oval on Jupiter's southern side in eighteen thirty-one. Others noticed it too, and the pictures began to agree with each other.

By the middle of the century, the spot was no longer a rumor. It had a place and a shape, and observers could find it again from night to night. Slowly, a sense settled in that this was a lasting thing.

And it was not the spot we see now.

In those old drawings, the feature is long. In the late eighteen hundreds it was about twice as long as it is today, stretched like a lozenge along its band of cloud. Roughly three Earths could have fit inside it, side by side.

Its color was different too. In eighteen seventy-eight, it flushed a strong brick red, and people wrote about it in newspapers. Then the color faded, and came back, and faded again, over the following decades.

This is where the work of historians begins. Today, a few researchers sit with old sketches laid beside modern measurements. They check where the spot sat, how fast it drifted, and how long it was.

It is slow, patient work. A drawing is only as good as the eye and the hand that made it, and a seventeenth century sketch has no scale at all.

Still, their results have a shape. One careful study concluded that the spot Cassini saw was probably not the one we have now. The older spot may have faded away, and a newer storm may have formed later, in the eighteenth or nineteenth century.

Other researchers are less sure. The records are so thin, they say, that a single storm lasting nearly four hundred years cannot be ruled out. It would be a storm older than the United States.

That is where the evidence stands. Observers have recorded a spot on Jupiter since the seventeenth century.

Yet the storm of today may not be that one.

What we can say is this. A continuous record of the red spot reaches back to the eighteen-thirties. That is almost two hundred years of one storm turning in the same place. No hurricane on Earth has ever lasted much longer than a month.

And so the question changes shape. We may not know how old the spot truly is, but we can ask how a storm survives even for two centuries. For that, we have to leave the old sketches behind, and go down into the clouds.

chapters.title: Falling Into the Clouds
chapters.question: What would you see if you sank into the storm?
chapters.reveal: The spot rises several kilometers above the neighboring clouds, and Juno's measurements show its roots extend about three hundred to five hundred kilometers below.
beats: Begin in the thin, cold upper haze of Jupiter
The storm's cloud tops stand higher and colder than their surroundings
Pressure and temperature rise as we sink
Juno's microwave radiometer sees into the deep atmosphere
The storm reaches far deeper than the water clouds
Darkness, pressure, and no solid floor below
image_queries: Jupiter Great Red Spot Juno close
chapters.text:
The air up here is almost nothing. At the very top of Jupiter's atmosphere, the haze is thin, cold, and pale, and the light from the distant Sun comes in sideways, soft and orange. There is no ground to stand on, only a slow drift downward. And somewhere below us, a storm is waiting.

So what would you see if you sank into it?

At first, very little changes. The haze thickens a little, like breath on a window. Then, ahead and below, the cloud deck begins to rise. It is not a hole in the planet, as it can look from far away. It is a hill of cloud, and its top stands well above everything around it.

Measurements say the Great Red Spot towers several kilometers higher than the clouds beside it. That is a good fraction of the height of Earth's tallest mountains. And the summit is colder than its surroundings, because the air there has been lifted into thinner, chillier layers. A high, cold cloud top is what a high-pressure storm looks like from the side.

Now we sink. Slowly, the air gets heavier. The pressure climbs, and so does the temperature. Where the pressure equals what we feel at the surface of the Earth, the air is already about as cold as a winter night in Antarctica. A little deeper, it becomes mild. Deeper still, it grows hot, and the light from above fades to a deep brown.

We cannot actually fall this way, of course. No probe has ever flown into the Great Red Spot. The only craft that ever dived into Jupiter's atmosphere, the Galileo probe in nineteen ninety-five, entered far from the storm. It lasted only about an hour.

Yet we know something about what lies beneath the Spot. The knowledge comes from a spacecraft that never touches the clouds at all.

It is called Juno. It circles Jupiter in a long, looping orbit, and every few weeks it swings low over the cloud tops. On board is an instrument called a microwave radiometer. It does not take pictures. It listens, in a way, to faint radio glow rising from deep inside the planet.

Different wavelengths of that glow come from different depths. Long waves travel up from far below. Short waves come from nearer the top. By comparing them, scientists can build a slice through the atmosphere, layer by layer, as a doctor might read a scan.

When Juno passed over the Great Red Spot in two thousand nineteen, that slice looked unlike anything on Earth.

Jupiter has clouds made of water, far below the visible tops. On Earth, storms are shallow things, a thin skin on the air. The Great Red Spot is not. Its roots go down far past the water clouds.

Juno's measurements show the storm reaching at least three hundred kilometers below the cloud tops, and perhaps as far as five hundred.

That is roughly the distance from one large city to the next, but pointed straight down. It means the Spot is not a surface feature at all. It is a column of turning gas, far deeper than it is tall.

Let us follow the column down once more. The brown light is gone now. There is no sunrise here, no horizon, nothing to measure distance by. The pressure is crushing, far beyond even the deepest ocean trench on Earth. The gas around us is hot and dense, and slowly thickening, yet nowhere does it turn into a floor.

Jupiter has no ground. The air simply becomes denser and denser, until it behaves less like a gas and more like a fluid, and goes on that way, deeper than any instrument can see.

A storm that deep is not easily pushed over. It holds a great weight of turning air, and it is held in turn by the world beneath it. Which raises a better question than how deep it goes. What keeps it spinning at all, century after century, when every storm we know on Earth runs out of strength within days?

chapters.title: Why a Storm Can Last for Centuries
chapters.question: On Earth, hurricanes die within weeks, so why does this one persist?
chapters.reveal: Jupiter has no land to drag a storm to a halt, and the Great Red Spot keeps itself alive by absorbing the smaller storms that drift into it.
beats: How hurricanes on Earth fade over land and cold water
Jupiter has no continents and no ocean surface
Jet streams on either side of the spot hold it between them
Smaller vortices are swallowed and feed the larger one
Internal heat from Jupiter keeps the atmosphere turning
Open question: how the storm will evolve and for how long
chapters.text:
A hurricane on Earth has a short life. It forms over warm water, grows for a few days, and then begins to come apart. Most are gone within a week or two.

Some of the longest ever recorded lasted about a month. Then they, too, fell apart, as every one of them does.

Now look at the great red oval turning below us. People have watched it for almost two centuries, and perhaps much longer. The same kind of spinning storm, yet it has not stopped. Why does this one persist?

Start with how an Earth hurricane dies. It feeds on warm ocean water, drawing heat and moisture up from the surface. When it drifts over cold water, the fuel runs out. When it crosses a coastline, it loses the ocean altogether. Hills, forests and towns drag at the bottom of the storm, and the spinning slows like a wheel with a hand pressed against it.

So an Earth storm is always fighting its own surroundings. Sooner or later, the ground or the cold sea wins.

Jupiter offers no such opponent. There are no continents here. There is no coast, no mountain range, no shallow sea. The atmosphere simply grows denser as it goes down, gas blending into hotter and thicker gas, with no surface to scrape against.

The Great Red Spot has nothing to run aground on.

That removes the thing that kills our storms. But it does not explain what keeps this one alive. A storm with no brake can still spread out and fade, like a ripple on a pond.

Here the bands we saw from far away matter. Jupiter's clouds are stretched into stripes, and the stripes are moving. On the northern side of the spot, a jet stream blows toward the west. On the southern side, another blows toward the east. The two currents run in opposite directions, and the spot sits between them.

Picture two rivers flowing past each other, with a slow whirlpool in the gap. The opposing flows roll the whirlpool like a ball between two palms. They keep it spinning, and they keep it from drifting away or spreading thin.

There is a second source of strength. Jupiter is crowded with smaller storms. Many are only a few hundred kilometers across, tiny beside the giant. They form in the bands, and they are carried along by the winds. Some of them drift toward the spot.

Astronomers have watched this happen in images from Hubble and from spacecraft. A small vortex comes close, is stretched, and is pulled in. Sometimes it passes through the edge of the great storm and is gone within days. Researchers think each such meeting gives the larger storm a little of the smaller one's spin.

The Great Red Spot survives because it eats the storms that drift too near.

It is not a perfect feast. Models suggest the spot may lose more energy to friction with the surrounding winds than it gains. But the meals seem to help. They may be part of the reason it has not faded.

One more ingredient sits underneath everything. Jupiter is still warm from its birth. It gives off about one and a half times the heat it takes from the Sun, and that heat rises from the deep interior all the time. Warm gas climbs, cooler gas sinks, and the whole atmosphere keeps turning over. On Earth, the Sun does nearly all of this work. On Jupiter, the planet itself does much of it.

So the engine does not shut off at night, or in winter, or when the storm drifts somewhere unlucky. It simply runs.

None of this means the storm is permanent. It is shrinking, and the reasons are not fully understood. It could break into smaller storms. It could settle into a smaller, steadier shape. Or it could stay for centuries more. Nobody knows which, and the models do not agree.

What we do know is that the storm has been losing size for as long as we have measured it. And that raises a question about the spot's edges, and about how much of it is left to lose.

chapters.title: The Shrinking Red Spot
chapters.question: Is the great storm slowly fading away?
chapters.reveal: Measurements show the spot has shrunk from spanning more than three Earths in the late nineteenth century to a bit more than one, and it has become rounder.

The shape changing from a long oval to a rounder one
Hubble's repeated pictures tracking the change
Possible reasons are still debated
Open question: will the storm shrink into something smaller or stabilize
image_queries: Jupiter Hubble Great Red Spot comparison
chapters.text:
An observer sits at an eyepiece in the autumn of eighteen seventy-eight, sketching a red oval on a page. By their reckoning, the spot is about forty thousand kilometers long.

That is a hard number to hold in the mind. It is roughly the distance around the whole Earth at the equator. Three Earths, set end to end, could have fit inside that single storm.

Now look at the same place today. The oval is still there, still red, still turning. But it seems smaller than those old drawings suggest. So is the great storm slowly fading away?

Measurements from the nineteenth century were made by eye, with a small mark on a glass and a steady hand. They were good for their time. Different observers gave different widths, but they agreed on the main point. The spot was enormous, and it was long and narrow, like a stretched egg lying on its side.

The first close measurements came in the late nineteen seventies. Two Voyager spacecraft flew past Jupiter within a few months of one another. Their cameras recorded the spot as a sharp, detailed shape, and astronomers could finally measure its width from real pictures. It was already smaller, spanning roughly two Earths.

Then the Hubble Space Telescope took over the watch. Since the early nineteen nineties, it has photographed Jupiter again and again, year after year, with the same eye and the same care. Each image is a single frame. Together they are a slow film of a storm changing shape.

The film shows two things. The spot keeps getting shorter, and it keeps getting rounder. The long oval of the old drawings has been gradually drawn in at both ends. Today the storm looks less like a stretched egg and more like a plate, set a little wider than tall.

Its length has been shrinking by a small amount every year. In the early two thousands, the change looked slow. In the following years it seemed to speed up for a while. Put into a human scale, it is like a lake whose shore moves a little each spring, too little to notice in a day, but plain over a lifetime.

Then came the numbers that seemed to settle the matter.

Measurements show the spot has shrunk from about three Earths wide to a bit more than one.

That is a loss of about two thirds of its length in a century and a half. Most of that change has happened in a single human lifetime of careful watching.

Why? Here, honestly, nobody is certain. One idea says the jet streams on either side of the spot have shifted, squeezing the storm from north and south. Another says the storm is absorbing fewer of the smaller vortices that once fed it, so it is losing more than it gains. A third looks at the spot's height. As it shrinks sideways, it seems to grow taller, and that may change how the winds inside it behave.

Each idea explains some of what the pictures show. None of them explains all of it. The deep atmosphere that drives the storm is hidden under clouds, and we have only started to look inside.

There is also the matter of the early drawings. If the spot seen in the eighteen hundreds was a different storm from this one, then the shrinking we measure may be only one chapter in a longer story. A storm can be born, grow large, and shrink again, and Jupiter may do this many times.

So what comes next? The spot might keep shrinking until it becomes a small, tight vortex, and perhaps fade altogether. Or it might settle at a smaller size and hold there for centuries more. Some of the numbers suggest the shrinking has slowed in recent years. Others suggest it has not.

For now, the red oval keeps its place, turning once every few Earth days. Its edges are closer than they used to be. And somewhere beneath those edges, the winds are still deciding what the storm will be.

chapters.title: The Hexagon of Saturn
chapters.question: Could a storm ever sit on a planet's pole and have six straight sides?
chapters.reveal: At Saturn's north pole, a hexagonal jet stream wider than two Earths has persisted for decades, with a hurricane-like vortex at its center.
beats: Leave Jupiter and cross to Saturn, a paler, quieter world
Voyager's first glimpse of a six-sided cloud pattern
Cassini flies over the pole and shows the vortex at its center
How the hexagon stays fixed while clouds move
Laboratory experiments that make polygon patterns in spinning fluids
Open question: precisely what holds the corners in place
chapters.text:
Saturn is quieter than Jupiter. Its face is pale gold, smooth as cream, with bands so faint you have to look twice to find them. After the red oval and its crowded edges, the calm is almost a relief. The light here is about one hundredth of what reaches Earth, and the cloud tops are colder than one hundred and seventy degrees below zero Celsius.

Nothing in these clouds suggests geometry. Storms are round, or stretched, or ragged. We expect them to be soft at the edges, like a swirl of milk in tea.

So the picture that came back in nineteen eighty-one was strange. Voyager one was passing the planet, and its cameras were pointed at the far north. There, around the pole, the clouds seemed to form a shape with straight sides. Voyager two saw it again nine months later.

Scientists looked at it for a long time. A ring of clouds, ruled with a straightedge, with six corners.

Could a storm ever sit on a planet's pole and have six straight sides?

For more than twenty years, no one could look closer. The pole stays in winter darkness for years at a time, and the spacecraft that followed flew by at too low an angle. Then the Cassini spacecraft arrived and settled into orbit around Saturn in two thousand and four. Its instruments could see heat as well as light, so the dark did not stop it. Later, its path was tilted to carry it high above the poles.

What it found was larger than anyone had pictured. The hexagon is a jet stream, a river of wind that runs around the pole. Each of its six sides is about as long as the diameter of Earth. Across the whole shape, you could fit about two Earths side by side.

And at its center, there was something else. A vortex, turning in the middle of the pole like the eye of a hurricane. Its clouds formed a wall, and the wall plunged down into a clear, dark center. The eye is about two thousand kilometers across, roughly the distance from Madrid to Moscow. Winds at its edge blow faster than any hurricane on Earth.

The hexagon is also very steady. Over decades, the clouds inside it have been carried around by the wind. But the corners themselves have barely moved. Cassini, and Voyager before it, measured the same turning rate for the shape, close to the length of a Saturn day as the deep interior spins. The clouds race. The pattern stays.

So the hexagon is a wave, not an object. Think of the ripple that stays fixed in a stream behind a rock. The water rushes through it, but the ripple stays put. Here, the wind rushes through the six corners and the shape remains.

Still, why six?

An answer came from a laboratory, and a very ordinary one. In the nineteen nineties and again in two thousand and ten, researchers filled a round tank with water and set it spinning on a turntable. Inside, a ring rotated a little faster than the fluid around it. At first the edge of the current was smooth. Then it began to wobble.

The wobble settled into a shape with corners. Slow the ring or speed it up, and the number of corners changed. Three, four, five, six. Triangles, squares, pentagons, all made from water, turning.

The experiment shows that a spinning current can carve straight lines into itself without anything solid to hold it. That is a real result. It tells us that the hexagon is not impossible, and not even strange, once the right conditions exist.

But a tank is not a planet. Saturn has no walls to keep the jet in place. The tank has no deep, hot, gaseous interior, and no sunlight fading through a long winter. Scientists still do not know exactly what fixes the corners where they are. Some think the answer lies deep below the clouds, in how the winds reach far into the planet. Others look to the way the jet bends against its neighbors.

For now, a great six-sided ring turns at the top of Saturn, and the cause is unfinished. And Saturn, it seems, has another way of making weather. One that arrives only rarely, and all at once.

chapters.title: Saturn's Great White Storms
chapters.question: Why does Saturn sometimes erupt with a storm that wraps the whole planet?
chapters.reveal: Roughly every Saturn year, a giant white storm breaks out and can grow until it encircles the planet, as Cassini watched in 2010 and 2011.
beats: Saturn's calm, butter-colored face
The great white storm that appeared in 2010
Cassini follows the head and the long tail growing around the planet
Lightning flashes seen in the storm
Ammonia and water-rich clouds rising from below
Open question: what triggers these eruptions so rarely
chapters.text:
Late in the year twenty ten, the astronomers who watch Saturn through Earth's telescopes noticed something wrong with its face. A small white mark had appeared in the northern hemisphere, where nothing had been the day before.

Until then, the planet had looked the way it always does. Soft bands of pale gold and cream, laid one above another, with almost no contrast between them. Seen from far away, it could be a painted ball of butter. Nothing on it seems to move.

Then the white mark began to grow. And a question came with it. Why does a planet this quiet sometimes erupt with a storm that wraps all the way around it?

The Cassini spacecraft was already there, in orbit, close enough to look. Its cameras watched the bright spot spread over days and then weeks. The front of the storm, the head, pushed on in one direction. Behind it, a long tail of white cloud stretched out and followed.

The head moved with the planet's winds. The tail kept lengthening. In a few months the storm was wide enough that Earth would have fit inside it many times over. By the following year, the tail had reached around the whole planet and met the head again.

Saturn was wearing a belt of cloud, circling its entire northern middle. That is a distance longer than a hundred thousand kilometers, and you would not walk it in a lifetime of walking.

It took a long time to fade. The pale scar was still visible for months afterward, stretched and slowly smoothing, until the winds had mixed it into the bands around it.

And inside the storm, there was light.

Cassini's instruments picked up flashes, and so did cameras on the night side of the planet. Lightning was flickering through the clouds, far more often than on Earth. Each bolt is enormous, many times stronger than what we see in our own sky. On Saturn, thunderstorms can rage for weeks, and the radio crackle from them can be heard from space.

Lightning needs water. That was the first hint of what lay below.

The white clouds themselves were made of ammonia ice, frozen crystals of a gas you might know from household cleaners. Ammonia normally sits deep beneath the visible cloud tops, hidden under a haze. Here, it had been carried upward, fast and in bulk. Spectrometers also found signs of water ice mixed in, from still deeper down.

So the storm was a kind of fountain. Warm, moist air rose from far beneath the surface, through layers that normally stay calm, and burst out into the cold above. It punched through the quiet haze and spread across the sky.

Over many years, Saturn seems to hold that moisture down below. The deep layer of water clouds gets heavier and heavier, and the air above it stays sealed, like a lid. Then, at some point, the lid gives way.

Giant white storms break out on Saturn roughly once every Saturn year, which is about thirty Earth years. Astronomers have recorded them in eighteen seventy-six, nineteen thirty-three, nineteen ninety, and twenty ten. Cassini watched the last one from beginning to end, as it grew until it encircled the planet.

Why that rhythm? Nobody knows for certain. The deep water may build up slowly, until the layer becomes unstable. The slow change of seasons on Saturn, as it leans toward and away from the Sun, may play a part. Neither idea has been proven.

Think of how rare this is. In one human lifetime, a person might see only two or three of these storms. Most people on Earth will never look up and know that one is under way.

And yet the planet that makes them has more to show, in the places where its light is hardest to catch. Out beyond Saturn, the Sun is a bright star and little more. The next worlds are colder, darker, and farther than anything yet.

chapters.title: Winds at the Edge of the Sun's Reach
chapters.question: Do the farthest planets, faint and cold, still have weather?
chapters.reveal: Neptune, which receives almost no sunlight, has some of the fastest winds measured in the solar system, and its dark storms appear and vanish in only a few years.
beats: Travel outward to Uranus, pale blue-green and tilted on its side
Uranus shows few storms, but Hubble and Webb find bright clouds and a polar cap
Voyager 2 finds Neptune's Great Dark Spot in 1989
Hubble later sees that spot gone and new ones appear elsewhere
Neptune's supersonic winds measured in its clouds
Open question: how so distant a planet can power such weather
chapters.text:
Out past Saturn, the Sun shrinks to a point of light. At Uranus it is nearly four hundred times fainter than it is on Earth. Noon there would feel like deep twilight.

Uranus itself looks calm. It is a pale blue-green ball, smooth as a polished stone. And it lies tipped on its side, rolling around the Sun like a barrel, so that each pole faces the Sun for decades at a time. When Voyager two flew past in nineteen eighty-six, the cameras found almost nothing to look at. A few faint clouds, and little else.

So here is the question. Do the farthest planets, faint and cold, still have weather?

For Uranus, the answer came slowly. Later, Hubble watched it year after year and caught bright clouds drifting through its atmosphere. Some were made of methane ice, high and white against the blue. The Webb telescope then looked in infrared light and saw something new. Over the pole that faces the Sun, a bright cap of haze, like a pale hood. Near its edge, a ring of small, bright storms.

Uranus, then, is not dead. It is quiet, and that is a different thing. Its weather is thin and slow, and it takes patient eyes to find it.

Then Voyager two kept going, three more years, across a distance that no other spacecraft has crossed since. In August of nineteen eighty-nine, it reached Neptune.

Neptune is a deeper blue than Uranus, a color like ink in clear water. And on its southern side, the cameras found a dark oval. It was about as wide as Earth. Around it ran streaks of white cloud, stretched out like brushstrokes. Scientists named it the Great Dark Spot, and they thought they had found a cousin of Jupiter's storm.

They had not quite. In nineteen ninety-four, Hubble turned toward Neptune and looked for the spot.

It was gone.

Nothing remained of it. Not a smudge, not a shadow. A storm as large as our world had faded away in a few years. Not long afterward, a new dark spot appeared in the northern half of the planet. Others have come since, and left again. Some lasted a couple of years, some a little longer. Compare that with Jupiter's storm, which has turned for centuries.

The winds are stranger still. Astronomers measure them by following the clouds from one picture to the next. On Neptune, the fastest gusts reach roughly two thousand kilometers an hour. That is faster than the speed of sound in the air we breathe, and about nine times the strength of the worst hurricane on Earth. Yet the air on Neptune is so thin and cold that you would feel it more as a push than a roar.

And this is the strange part. Neptune sits about thirty times farther from the Sun than we do. It receives almost no sunlight at all.

Its winds are among the fastest ever measured in the solar system.

Where does the energy come from? Neptune does give off more heat than it takes in, so some warmth must rise from deep inside. But that is not a full answer. Other planets have heat too, and their winds are slower. Cold air may also meet less friction there, letting the wind run free. Scientists have ideas, but no one can yet say for sure. How can so distant a planet power weather like this?

For now, it keeps turning, far out in the dark. A faint blue point, with storms that come and go. And all the while, the same three ingredients, found again and again on every giant world we have seen.

chapters.title: The Weather of Every World
chapters.question: What does a storm tell us about the planet it lives on?
chapters.reveal: The same laws of spinning, heated air shape every storm we know, from a hurricane on Earth to a world-wide whirl on Jupiter, and Webb now lets us watch weather on planets around other stars.
beats: Return to the sweep of all four giant planets
Rotation, heat, and a deep atmosphere as the ingredients of every storm
Earth's hurricanes compared in miniature
Webb and Hubble reading clouds and winds on planets around other stars
Juno and later missions continuing to probe Jupiter's depths
Come back to the Great Red Spot, still turning as the camera drifts away
chapters.text:
A telescope on a mountain in Chile turns toward a star that has no name, only a catalogue number. The star is far too dim to see with the eye. But beside it, something faint is passing in front, and the light is changing.

Astronomers have learned to read that change. When starlight slips through the air of a distant planet, some colors are taken out of it. What remains is a kind of fingerprint, written in water, in sand, in haze.

So here is a quiet question. What does a storm tell us about the planet it lives on?

We have now seen four of them up close. Jupiter, with its red eye, turning for centuries. Saturn, with its six-sided crown and its rare white storms. Uranus, pale and mostly still. Neptune, with dark spots that come and go in the blue.

They look nothing alike. Yet they share a pattern. Each one is a large ball of gas, spinning fast, warmed from below, with no ground to slow the air.

Rotation is the first ingredient. Jupiter turns once in about ten hours, so a day there is shorter than a night's sleep. That spin bends every moving current into a circle, and stretches the winds into long bands.

Heat is the second. Deep inside, each giant still holds warmth left from its birth, and Jupiter and Saturn give off more than they receive from the Sun. Warm gas rises, cool gas sinks, and the air never rests.

The third is depth. An atmosphere thousands of kilometers thick has room to build a storm that can stretch, and settle, and stay.

Earth has all three, only smaller. A hurricane is born over warm water, spinning with the planet, fed by heat rising from the sea. The strongest ones can be about the width of a country like Spain. The Great Red Spot, at its widest, could hold Earth itself.

But the laws are the same. Air that spins and rises will gather into a vortex, if nothing stops it.

On Earth, something always does. A hurricane crosses a coast, and its fuel is gone within days. On Jupiter there is no coast.

The same laws shape every storm we know.

That idea has now left our own system. The James Webb Space Telescope looks at planets circling other stars, and it can split their light into thin slices of color. In some, it has found water vapor. In others, clouds of sand, and the signs of sulfur made by sunlight in the upper air.

Hubble helped to begin this work, and Webb has carried it much further. On some of these worlds, astronomers have measured how the temperature changes from one side to the other. On a few, they have seen signs of winds, carrying heat around the planet at speeds no hurricane has ever reached.

We cannot see a distant storm as a picture. But we can see that the air is moving, and that the clouds are changing. Weather, it turns out, is not a local habit of Earth. It is what happens whenever a world has air and a fire to stir it.

Closer to home, the study goes on. The Juno spacecraft still circles Jupiter, passing low over the clouds, listening to the deep atmosphere with its instruments. Each pass shows a little more of what lies beneath the red. Later missions may go further, perhaps reaching into the layers where pressure grows too great to picture.

Nobody yet knows exactly how deep the roots of the storm go, or how long it will last. That question is still open. It may be answered in our lifetimes, or in someone else's.

Now the camera lifts away. The bands of Jupiter grow narrow, cream and rust and white. The planet shrinks, and the great oval at its southern edge becomes a single red mark.

It is still turning. It was turning before the first telescope, and before anyone looked up and wrote it down.

Down here, a gentle wind moves across a sleeping field. It is made of the same laws. The same turning, the same warmth, the same patient air.

You have crossed a long way tonight, through clouds and cold and light. There is nothing left to chase. Let the planets keep turning, as they always have.

Goodnight.

cold_open:
A storm wider than Earth has been turning in Jupiter's clouds for at least one hundred and fifty years.

We thought it was a surface mark, a red eye painted on a distant world. But the newest measurements say it is shrinking. They also say it reaches far deeper than anyone expected.

How does a storm last for centuries? What keeps it alive?

Tonight, we drift toward Jupiter until its stripes become rivers of cloud. We fall into the storm itself. Then we cross to Saturn, to a hexagon of wind at its pole and white storms that wrap the whole planet.

Nothing here is rushed. Every image is real, and every word is true.

There is nothing for you to do but listen.

Let's begin with the eye of Jupiter.

topic: Jupiter's Great Red Spot and the storms of the giant planets

shorts.title: A Storm Wide Enough to Swallow Earth
shorts.narration: There is a storm on Jupiter wide enough to swallow our entire planet, and it has been turning for almost two centuries. It is called the Great Red Spot. Today it measures a little over one Earth across, about thirteen thousand kilometers, roughly the distance from London to Sydney. Set our whole world down inside it, with its oceans, mountains and cities, and it would sit there like a stone in a bowl. Winds along its rim blow at hundreds of kilometers an hour, yet one full turn takes about six days. On Earth, a hurricane dies within a week or two. Jupiter has no coastline to end it. The full journey through the giant storms is waiting on the channel.

shorts.title: Saturn's Six-Sided Storm at the Pole
shorts.narration: At the top of Saturn sits a storm with six perfectly straight sides. Voyager first saw it in nineteen eighty-one, and scientists stared at it for a long time. A ring of clouds, ruled as if with a straightedge. Each side is about as long as the diameter of Earth, so two whole planets could fit across it. At its center turns a vortex with an eye about two thousand kilometers wide. The clouds race around the shape, yet the six corners barely move, like a ripple staying fixed in a stream behind a rock. Researchers can make hexagons in a spinning tank of water, but nobody knows exactly why Saturn holds this one. The full journey is waiting on the channel.
